# AI speak patterns, part 4

Built from the packs in `hooks/lib/patterns`. Each section names its own source.

The category index is in `ai-speak-patterns.md`.

## ai-tool-mention

Presets: `default`, `ryan`, `technical`, `git`, `all`. Source: Group G research: anthropics/claude-code#1296 and anthropics/claude-code#66602.

Names of AI coding tools, or the agent narrating its own process instead of the change.

| Flagged | Fix |
|---|---|
| `as requested by the user` | state the change directly |
| `per the user's instructions` | state the change directly |
| `per the assistant`, `per the model`, `per the AI` | state the change directly |
| `as suggested by the assistant`, `as suggested by the model`, `as suggested by the AI` | state the change directly |
| `the model suggested`, `the assistant wrote` | state the change directly |
| `AI-generated`, `AI generated` | cut the disclosure |
| `with AI assistance` | cut the disclosure |
| `generated by AI`, `written by an AI` | cut the disclosure |
| `generated by` or `written with` a named AI tool | cut the tool name |
| a `git commit` command naming an AI tool | cut the tool name |

A tool name reports only next to process wording (`generated by`, `written by`, `suggested by`) or inside a `git commit` command, so a comment that just names a tool stays clean. That wording around `the model` or `the assistant` reports as well, which a repo whose subject is model output drops with `disablePatterns`.

## benefit-tail

Presets: `ryan`, `technical`, `git`, `all`. Source: Group G research: AI-generated PR summary and commit body conventions.

A sentence ends in a justification clause tacked on after a comma.

| Flagged | Fix |
|---|---|
| `, which improves readability` and the like | cut the justification clause |
| `, making it easier to maintain` | cut the justification clause |
| `, for better performance` | cut the justification clause |
| `, ensuring consistency` | cut the justification clause |
| `, so that it's more robust` | cut the justification clause |

The noun list is intentionally abstract. A tail that names a measured effect, such as `cuts p99 latency to 90ms`, does not match.

## canned-review

Presets: `default`, `ryan`, `technical`, `git`, `all`. Source: Group G research: PR review boilerplate.

Stock PR-review phrasing used regardless of what the diff actually does.

| Flagged | Fix |
|---|---|
| `LGTM with minor nits` | cut, or approve plainly |
| `Looks good to me` | cut, or approve plainly |
| `Nice work` | cut |
| `Great work on this` | cut |
| `One small suggestion` | state the suggestion |
| `Minor nitpick` | state the point |
| `Overall, this looks good` | cut, or approve plainly |
| `solid implementation` | cut |
| `well-structured` | cut, or name the structure |
| `clean implementation` | cut |
| `It might be worth considering` | state the suggestion |

`Consider adding tests` and `I'd suggest` are left out. Careful reviewers open with them before a concrete point, which held the full list under 85% precision.

## file-narration

Presets: `ryan`, `technical`, `git`, `all`. Source: Group G research: git commit-message conventions and conventional commits.

Text narrates a trivial file operation instead of stating the change.

| Flagged | Fix |
|---|---|
| `This commit adds` | state the change, cut the frame |
| `This commit introduces` | state the change, cut the frame |
| `This PR introduces` | state the change, cut the frame |
| `This PR adds` | state the change, cut the frame |
| `Here's what changed` | list the changes directly |
| `The file now contains` | state the content directly |
| `Added a new file called` | name the file, cut the frame |
| `I've updated the`, `I've added a` | state the change, cut the frame |
| a line opening with `Updated`, `Added`, or `Deleted` plus a file name | use the imperative mood |

The past-tense form has to open the line, so a conventional-commit subject such as `docs: update README` stays clean.

## praise-sandwich

Presets: `ryan`, `git`, `all`. Source: Group G research: Wikipedia compliment sandwich, Radical Candor feedback sandwich.

Review or reply text opens and closes with praise around a middle critique.

| Flagged | Fix |
|---|---|
| Review or reply text opens and closes with praise around a middle critique. | `minParagraphs = 3`, `minWords = 18` |

Needs praise in the first and last paragraph and a critique marker between them. People are taught this shape too, so the pack stays out of the `default` preset.

## hidden-characters

Presets: `default`, `ryan`, `technical`, `git`, `all`. Source: Opus 5.5 replies (U+2011 at 0.33 per 10,000 words), Microsoft known issue on LLM hyphens (Apr 2026), OpenAI U+202F reports (2025), Trojan Source bidi controls, Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing.

Invisible or look-alike characters that model output and chat UIs leave in text.

| Flagged | Fix |
|---|---|
| a zero-width space, zero-width non-joiner, word joiner, or Mongolian vowel separator | remove the zero-width character |
| a zero-width joiner outside an emoji sequence | remove the zero-width joiner |
| a byte order mark after the first character | remove the byte order mark |
| a soft hyphen or non-breaking hyphen | use `-`, or remove the soft hyphen |
| a narrow no-break space or figure space | use a plain space |
| a Unicode tag character | remove the tag character, it can hide text |
| a variation selector other than the emoji and text selectors | remove the variation selector, it can hide data |
| a bidirectional control character | remove the bidi control |
| ChatGPT citation markers: `cite` followed by `turn0search0`, or `contentReference` followed by an `oaicite` index | remove the citation residue |

Anthropic's text watermark adds no characters, so this pack cannot see it. In a code file the pack reads the whole file, string literals included, through the `code` scope. U+00A0 is left out: npm READMEs carry it 5.6 times per 10,000 words. A zero-width joiner inside an emoji sequence and tag characters after the black flag (subdivision flags) stay unflagged. A right-to-left project lists `hidden-characters` in `excludePacks` or drops the bidi row with its own pack.

## smart-punctuation

Presets: `default`, `ryan`, `technical`, `all`. Source: Group P research: Wikipedia, Signs of AI writing.

Curly quotes and the ellipsis character typical of text pasted from a chat UI.

| Flagged | Fix |
|---|---|
| a curly double quote | use a straight double quote |
| a curly opening single quote | use a straight single quote |
| a curly apostrophe | use a straight apostrophe |
| an ellipsis character | use three periods |

Prose files are intentionally out of scope: a whole-file scan re-reports typeset quotes that a person committed once. A project that wants `files` coverage overrides the pack.

## unicode-glyphs

Presets: `default`, `ryan`, `technical`, `all`. Source: Group P research: Wikipedia, Signs of AI writing.

Arrows, box drawing, dingbats, and geometric symbols used in place of plain ASCII or words.

| Flagged | Fix |
|---|---|
| an arrow character | use `->` or `<-`, or words |
| a box-drawing character | use ASCII table characters |
| a dingbat or check mark | use `[x]`, `[ ]`, or words |
| a miscellaneous symbol | use plain words, drop the symbol |
| a bullet character | use `-` or `*` for list items |
| a geometric shape character | use plain words, drop the symbol |

Every range skips code points that are also `Extended_Pictographic`, so emoji stay with the `formatting` pack and the dash characters stay with `em-dash`. Prose files stay out of scope for the same reason as `smart-punctuation`. Code comments are out of scope too: a measured pass over 797 library files found arrows in JSDoc examples and box-drawing type diagrams in hand-written comments, and the pack cannot tell those from decoration.
